Propterea uespere

The End of the First Book of Our Polygraphy

We rejoice that the end of the first book of our Polygraphy is at hand; by it, made readier for the matters that remain, we judge that the powers of our talent must be tested. For newly invented things sometimes trouble the beginner, because the one whom all follow has no one preceding him. The first beginning of any invention is the more difficult; afterwards, when it has been made firm, it brings greater confidence to the author. Therefore, completing the first book of our invention with God’s favor and help, we have divided the whole into three hundred eighty-four minutiae, assigning to each, in order, as is seen, its proper degrees of periphrases. And these form a sufficiently beautiful Christian harmony: sixteen different stations, with two hundred and nine thousand phrases duly joined together in all respects. Nothing is lacking here for students of these inventions of ours, so that in mystical, secret, and hidden matters, even those to be announced more remotely with the greatest safety, they may have the fullest knowledge and faculty. All things that are contained in the circle of the art proceed from a point; their atoms constitute a circular line, and, by a multitude of light, a straight one. Whatever is outside the line is said always to be enclosed among the minutiae and paraphrases, and never goes out. Therefore, whenever you have crossed the straight line of the day and have not fulfilled the purpose of the nocturnal syntax, turn the head back to the tail, and, once a joining has been made, let there be a binding of both to one another. Arrange the shadow in such a way that it does not confuse the sun by similarity of sound. Nor should you fear shame if, in the first calculation, the day has not comprehended the shadow; count it together with the other until the necessary proportion follows according to your wish. You will also be able to make a leap from the first to the second, knowing that in the first creation of days there was evening and morning, one day. Therefore, in the evening

51
consummato, diem reduc in sequentem, & signo dato per punctum binario simul monadi notū fige mysterium. Verum quo hanc euitare difficultatem possis, orbis nostri totius, magnas reuolutiones per gradus distingue arithmeticos, ubi dies pro nocte repetitur, nota Archimedis impone uolanti, ne ternarius immaturus reditū ad unitatē binario intercludat. Nam propterea minutias singularibus operātema labore numerandi paraphrasmata leuaremus. Si fueris industrius, diligēs studiosus in his quae ut artis principia nouae tradidimꝰ, crede nobis maiora inuenies latentia q̄ nos polliciti sumus. Enimuero cum inhis naturalia plura contineantur arcana, unū scias non ultimū, quod metatheseos operatione prudenti, etiam cuminumoles peritissimū in hac arte facies ignarū, uidentem caecumdoctū imperitū. Sifalsa Hebraeoꝝ esset uera opinio, orbium decem octomilium hominibus singulis, ista adinuentio nostra singulos daret modos tuto secrete scribendi ac nunciādi latissime quaecumque latine uellēt arcana. FINIS LIBRI primi polygraphiae adest, Ioannis Tritemij, abbatis monasterij sancti Iacobi apostolii, Vuirciburgensis xij. die mensis Februarias. Anno dominicae nativitate tis Millesimo quingētesimo octauo. IOANNIS TRITE- MII ABBATIS PEAPOLITANI ORDINIS SAN CTI BÉNEDICTI, POLYGRAPHIAE LIBER SECVNDVS CAPIT INITIVM. <Initial type="decorated-drop">R</Initial>ATIO numerandi mortalium, arte na turam conatur imitari monadis nullũ calculũ admittentis. Vnde q̃uis insti¬ tutio libri polygraphiae praecedẽtis ꝑ extensionem metathesinꝙ particula¬ rium, quasi ad uniuerfalía huius artis sufficiat in infinitas numeri progressiones, certa nos tamẽ consyderatio permouit, ut alteri copulemus. Lu¬ cis est in utroque dispar conditio, nõx uero cursus sui ordi¬ nem utrobique inuolatum custodit. Qui prudẽs est lector ex paruis et amp; non satis ad amussim politis adinuentionib⁹ nostris, facile maiora politioraque ingenio praestanti si ui¬ geat poterit inuenire. Quicquid est uisibile in uniuerso mundi circulo positum, adhuius nouae artis nostrae mini¬ sterium promtpum tribuit fulcimentum. Aer et amp; ignis, aq̃ &amp; terra, fontes et amp; flumĩa, arbores et amp; fructcta, flores et amp; gra¬ mina, uerba et amp; nomina, accidens et amp; substantia, lapides et arena, fimus et amp; stercora, res et amp; uocabula, bonesta et amp; uere¬ cunda, ligna et amp; metalla, dura et amp; liquida, existentia et amp; non existentia, historia et amp; fabula, homines et amp;iumenta, singula et amp; uniuerfa, quae uel sermo potest ex¬ primere, uel anima cogitate, campum polygraphiae no¬ strae praestant latiffimum, &amp; artem quantum mortalibus potest constare promittunt ampliandam fore in infinitũ. Nam sicuti ex unitate per binarium ternarius perfectum numerum in quaternario generat, sic huius adinuentio/

when it has been completed, bring the day back into the following one, and, when the sign has been given by a point, fix the mystery known to the binary together with the monad.

But in order that you may be able to avoid this difficulty, distinguish the great revolutions of our whole sphere by arithmetical degrees; where the day is repeated in place of the night, set the mark of Archimedes upon the flying thing, lest the untimely ternary, on its return to unity, be shut off by the binary. For on this account we would relieve [unclear] the paraphrases of counting by single minutiae. If you are industrious, diligent, and studious in these things which we have handed down as the principles of a new art, believe me, you will find greater things hidden there than we have promised. Indeed, since many natural secrets are contained in these things, know one thing, not the least: that by the prudent operation of metathesis, whenever you wish, you will make even one most skilled in this art ignorant, the seeing man blind, the learned man unskilled. If the false opinion of the Hebrews were true, namely that there are eighteen thousand worlds for each individual human being, this invention of ours would give to each one individual ways of safely and secretly writing and very widely communicating whatever secrets they wished in Latin.

The end of the first book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Apostle at Wurzburg, is here, on the twelfth day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord's nativity one thousand five hundred and eight.

Here begins the second book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of [Peapolitan?], of the Order of Saint Benedict.

The reckoning-method of mortals, by art, tries to imitate nature, which admits no calculation of the monad. Hence, although the arrangement of the preceding book of the Polygraphy, through the extension and metathesis of particular things, may suffice as it were for the universals of this art in the infinite progressions of number, nevertheless a certain consideration has moved us to join another to it. The condition of light is different in each; but night preserves inviolate in both the order of its course. The prudent reader, from these small inventions of ours, not sufficiently polished to the rule, will easily be able, if he is strong in excellent talent, to discover greater and more polished things. Whatever visible thing is set within the whole circle of the universe supplies ready support for the service of this new art of ours. Air and fire, water and earth, springs and rivers, trees and fruits, flowers and grasses, words and names, accident and substance, stones and sand, dung and excrements, things and terms, honorable and modest things, wood and metals, hard and liquid things, things existing and non-existing, history and fable, men and beasts of burden, particular and universal things, whatever speech can express or the soul can think, provide a very broad field for our Polygraphy, and promise that the art, so far as it can be established for mortals, will be enlarged to infinity. For just as from unity through the binary the ternary generates the perfect number in the quaternary, so the invention of this

52
nis consumatio per quaternarium in binario bis perfecto constituens radicem infinitum nobis numerum sub mi- nucijs rerum &; paraphrasmatũ polygraphiae donat. Nã et amp; si apud nos omnia nostra sint terminabilia, plura tamen saepius occurrũt quaenobis propter intellectus nostri tar- ditatem uidentur infinita. Guttas maris dinumerare quis poterit? Et cor homĩs inscrutabile quis penetrabit? Quẽ- admodum finitus et amp; circumscriptibilis numerus, ꝓgressi one ducibilis est in infinitum, sic huius artis institutio ua- ria metathesi ampliatur in immensum. Quicquid uspiam in toto mundo cernitur, nostrae institutioni per omnia cõ formatur, nec est aliquid nobis cognitũ quod uacet a my- sterio, si modus intelligitur a magistro. Nos autem ratio- ne persuasi sub ministerio binarij consistimus, &amp; partẽ to tius minimam breuiter explicamus. Neqꝫ ut conatũ erige remus ad grauiora nobis datur occasio, quae si nobis offe ratur acceptabilis, non aspernabimur cupiéntibus facere manifesta. Scriptum est enim: Vbi non est auditus ne sermonem effuderis unꝙͣ. Secundum igitur polygra- phiaelibrum adjicientes primo, formam eiusdem tenem⁹ et amp; modum. paraphrasmata in lumine diei octo et amp; trecẽta simplici progressione locantes promemoria honorabili, castissimae dei geniticis, quae si tempus affuisset oportu- num et amp; uenustiora dare poteramus, &amp; sufficiente diffusio ne campestri latiora. Sed utrũqꝫ facile dabit studiosa po- steritas, ut et amp; nitorem apponat materiae, &amp; sufficien̄te pro gressum formae. Primus cuiuslibet artis inuentor maiora transmittit ad posteros, quia cum sint artis dura et amp; incon- fueta principia, nulla reperitur subtilis adinuentio ab ori- gine consummata. Ex Peapoli quae et amp; Herbipolis urbe Francorum orientalium, duodecima die mēsis Februarij. Anno domini. ...the completion through the quaternary in the twice-perfect binary, establishing the root, grants us an infinite number under the minutiae of things and of the paraphrases of polygraphy. For even if among us all our things are terminable, nevertheless many things very often occur which, because of the slowness of our understanding, seem infinite to us. Who will be able to count the drops of the sea? And who will penetrate the inscrutable heart of man? Just as a finite and circumscribable number can be led by progression into infinity, so the instruction of this art is enlarged immeasurably by varied transposition. Whatever is seen anywhere in the whole world is in all respects conformed to our instruction; nor is there anything known to us that is free from mystery, if the method is understood from the master. But we, persuaded by reason, remain under the service of the binary, and briefly explain the smallest part of the whole. Nor is occasion given us to raise our undertaking to weightier matters; if it is offered to us as acceptable, we shall not refuse to make them manifest to those who desire it. For it is written: Where there is no hearing, never pour out speech. Therefore, adding the second book of Polygraphy to the first, we keep its form and method, placing three hundred and eight paraphrases in the light of day by simple progression, as an honorable memorial to the most chaste Mother of God. If a suitable time had been at hand, we could have given things both more elegant and, with sufficient broad spreading, more extensive. But studious posterity will easily provide both: that it may add polish to the material, and sufficient progress to the form. The first inventor of any art passes on greater things to posterity, because, since the beginnings of an art are hard and unfamiliar, no subtle invention is found perfected from its origin. From Peapolis, which is also Herbipolis, a city of the eastern Franks, on the twelfth day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508.

Nonne diui- sio corporum, & uarietas animorum? Nam ut veritas in euangelio protesta tur: Ex abundantia cordis os loquit̃. Lingua em̄ instrumentũ est eaꝝ cõce- ptionũ foras proferendi, quas apud semetipsum animus in interioribus cogitauit. Huius tamen ministerij secretorũ animi ad fensum plures funt modi, quoꝝ ꝓprietates usu uariant᷑ arte. Vfus ad placitũ introductus, cõmunis est multis: ars uero paucis. Deniqꝫ usus ipse loquendĩ nō re gulatus, quantum apud folos theutonicos infexcentis an- nis fit uariatus, nemo cito aestimabit, qui Otfridum Vuf- fenburgensem monachũ in carminibus linguae Germani- cae faepius non relegit. Mare fluit refluit, homines semel morientes nō amplius praesentẽ reuertuntur ad uitã. Succe dunt moribus mores, semp̃ ad molliora uigor animorũ mortalium decidit. Quis hodie apud Graecoꝝ priscos aemu latores germanos, antiqua idiomatũ tenet noticiã? Chro- nicis ueterũ historijs Francoꝝ Hunibaldus, Doracꝰ reliqui scriptores, q annis nos mille praecesserunt, multa ca crime prisco prosa sermonis theutonis suis synthema tibus dicta miscuerunt, quae hodie intelliguntur a paucis. Quid loquor de tẽporibus antiquis, cũ propriũ idioma no strum apud Francos orientales, Sueuos, Bauaros, Rhenen fes, Mosellanos, Colonienses, Saxones Doringos, nota bilem quotidię uariationem fuscipiat. With the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, savior of faithful souls, who lives in sacred trinal unity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, threefold in persons and one God in substance, incomprehensible, almighty, and everlasting, from whom, in whom, and through whom everything good, beautiful, and true proceeds, we have brought this book of Polygraphy to its end. To him be praise, honor, virtue, and glory for this, who through the innocence of his death freed our race from the destruction of eternal perdition, and by perpetual mercy opened again the entrance to eternal life for all who believe in him with a pure conscience. Line by line we have set down three hundred and eight paraphrases, avoiding, by [unclear] counsel, a more extended wandering digression. For at the beginning of this little work it seemed enough to us if we gave those who wished it cause to seek fuller things, since both time and reason failed us for them. Farewell, friendly reader. From Peapoli, on the penultimate day of the month of February, in the year of the Lord 1508.

The Second Book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot, is concluded by its end.

The Third Book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Peapoli, of the Order of Saint Benedict, begins.

What confounded the unity of language from the beginning of human creation? Was it not the division of bodies and the variety of minds? For as Truth declares in the Gospel: from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. For the tongue is the instrument for bringing outward those conceptions which the mind has thought within itself in its inner parts. Yet of this ministry of the mind's secrets to sense there are many modes, whose properties vary by practice and by art. Practice, introduced at pleasure, is common to many; art, however, to few. Finally, no one will quickly estimate how much the very practice of speaking, unregulated, has varied among the Teutons alone in six hundred years, unless he has often reread Otfrid, monk of Weissenburg, in his poems in the German tongue. The sea flows and flows back; men, once they have died, return no more to the present life. Customs succeed customs; the vigor of mortal minds always falls toward softer things. Who today, among the Germans, the ancient rivals of the Greeks, possesses knowledge of the old idioms? In chronicles and old histories of the Franks, Hunibald, Doracius, and the other writers who preceded us by a thousand years mixed many things, in old [unclear], said in the prose of the Teutonic language, into their compositions, which today are understood by few. Why do I speak of ancient times, when our own idiom among the Eastern Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, Rhinelanders, Mosellans, Cologne people, Saxons, Thuringians, undergoes notable variation every day? They are changed in time

re homines, uariantur &; mores, mutantur animi, uariãtur et amp; uestes: linguarũ alteratur simplicitas, prisca uariatur idiomatũ proprietas, nihil stabile reperitur in humanis. Omniū em̃ uicissitudo est rerũ, succedit uarietas simpli- citati animorũ. Quis defluẽtiã hac, ut ĩta loquar, perpetuã ad cõcordiã poterit reducere unitatis? Transeunt em̃ tẽpo- ra plura ut scriptura dicit, multiplex erit scientia. Quod aũt duobus Polygraphiae libris praecedentibus tertiũ adij cimus, ratione nō caruit speciali. Nā ut cũ uariae sint homi- nũ voluntates, recte multiples dantur modi ad honestas oꝑationes. In illis noctẽ dies illuminat, in istis uero dies a lumine uacat. Illic umbram lux circũducit in lumine, isthic aũt caecus caecũ illuminat, uisum sine oculis existẽs ꝑ- manens quē nō habet tenebris ministrat. Hic nox diẽ cali gine perpetua obnubilat, ambulãs in tenebris sine lumi ne caeco ducatũ praestat. Haec paraphrasmata cunctis ꝑ mũ dum hominibus deseruiũt, in omni lingua quodlibet ar chanũ, tuto, secure, ac sine periculo ad cabalisticũ binariũ transmittunt. Barbaris risum mouet latinitas, suspicio- nẽ latinis ipsa barbaries generat. Refert tamẽ nihil aut parũ quoniã suspicio quaniũlibet fuerit, mysteriũ nihilominus omne secretissimum cõtinebit. Ad mentẽ regulas praece pta quae tradidimus operator studiosus reuocet, ne inutili- ter inuanum sibi alijs laboret. Intelligentia enim opus est, sine qua nullius artis cõstabit utilitas. Iter paucis ostẽ dimus ad maxima, finitis modum dedimus ad infinita. Ex datis acceptis, facile maiora parantur amicis. Lector memento notam retrogradam in omni loco posse configi. quousque uotam apprehendas quietis. Vale, Ex Peapoli, prima die Martij. Anno domini. [unclear] men, and customs vary; minds change, and clothing too varies; the simplicity of languages is altered, the ancient propriety of idioms is varied; nothing stable is found among human things. For there is a vicissitude of all things; variety succeeds to the simplicity of minds. Who will be able to bring back this continual flowing-away, so to speak, to the concord of unity? For many times pass, as Scripture says: knowledge will be manifold. But that to the two preceding books of the Polygraphy we add a third has not lacked a special reason. For, since the wills of human beings are varied, varied methods are rightly given for honorable operations. In the former, night illumines the days; in these, however, day is without light. There light leads shadow around in light; here, however, a blind man illumines a blind man, and, being and remaining sight without eyes, ministers to the darkness what he does not have. Here night darkens the day with perpetual mist; walking in darkness, it offers blind guidance without light. These paraphrases serve all people throughout the world; in every language they transmit any secret safely, securely, and without danger to the cabalistic binary. Latinity moves barbarians to laughter; barbarism itself generates suspicion in Latins. Yet it matters nothing, or little, since however great the suspicion may have been, it will nonetheless contain every mystery most secretly. Let the diligent operator call back to mind the rules and precepts which we have handed down, lest he labor uselessly and in vain for himself and for others. For understanding is needed; without it the utility of no art will stand firm. In a few words we have shown the path to the greatest things; for finite things we have given a method toward infinite things. From things given and received, greater things are easily prepared for friends. Reader, remember that the retrograde sign can be fixed in every place, until you attain the desired rest. Farewell. From Peapoli, on the first day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

1056 QVOD IN principio tertij Polygragiae nostri operis sumus polliciti ad haben- dã glossae nouae umbrã et similitudinẽ corã inexpertis, laboris cõpendio satis fecimus ad exemplum. Noctẽ arcanis tuto seruientem, umbris periphrasma- tum ducẽdam cõmisimos, numeros ordine quatuor line arum telotenus interposuimus pro usu uolentiũ adaptatos Loca sunt minuti arum gradus habentia fixos triamilia cẽ rum quinquaginta, quanꝙ horarum restent momenta si uolueris infinita, pro secretandis in omni natione lingua orbis quicquid arcani occurrerit. Orbem linealiter nascen tem ex puncto, quotiens nox imaginem lucis excedit, quã tũ uolueris: opus fuerit reducere poteris ad semitã qua uenisti. Si noctis super est multum, reducito caudã draco- nis ad caudalicium originale in caput. Verũ binarius omni no sit certificatus de notis signaculis unitatis. Qui multũ esurit, multum laboret ut habeat quod manducet. Nec est est opus magni laboris id quorsum uolueris ducere, quod sua sponte progreditur. Hic ergo finem tertio poligraphiae nostrae libro constituimus, in nomine patris filij spiri- tus sancti. Lector mitis uale. Ex Peapolí, septima die men sis Martij. Anno domini Iesu Christi saluatoris nostri mil- lesimo quingentesimo octauo, Inditione undecima. Adest finis tertij libri Polygragiae Ioannis Trite mij abbatis Peapolitan̄ ordinis sancti Benedicti. What we promised at the beginning of the third book of our work Polygraphia, for obtaining the shadow and likeness of a new gloss before the inexperienced, we have sufficiently fulfilled by way of example in a compendium of labor. We have entrusted night, safely serving secrets, to be led through the shadows of periphrases; we have inserted numbers in the order of four lines down to the end, adapted for the use of those who wish. The places are degrees of minutiae, having fixed 3,150, although moments of hours remain, if you wish, infinite, for making secret in every nation and language of the world whatever secret matter may occur. The circle, arising linearly from a point, as often as night exceeds the image of light, by as much as you wish: if there is need, you will be able to bring the work back to the path by which you came. If there is much left over of night, bring back the dragon's tail to the original tail-place, into the head. But the pair must by all means be certified from the known signs of unity. He who hungers much should labor much, so that he may have something to eat. Nor is it a matter of great labor to lead wherever you wish that which advances of its own accord. Here, therefore, we set an end to the third book of our Polygraphia, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Gentle reader, farewell. From Peapoli, on the seventh day of the month of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ our Savior 1508, in the eleventh Indiction.

Here is the end of the third book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Peapoli, of the Order of Saint Benedict.

The fourth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Greater, Apostle, at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, begins.

The order of reason demanded that the fourth book of our Polygraphy be made unlike the preceding ones in character, invention, and ease, so that those wishing to share in the secrets of our matters may attain this not in one way, but by various and different ways. We have extended [the practice?], comprehensible by a very easy invention, so that the word, through the minutia always joined to the monad, may be recognized in the light in any order [unclear]. No distinction is found here between unity and the binary; nor will one who wishes to work need to have the instrument of the art at hand, since what follows the first without an intermediary reveals the hidden mystery. Hence the prudent, intelligent person, experienced in the science, will satisfy the operation at every time and place. The binary received from unity, whence it produces the ternary. The first recognition of this cryptology is easy at first sight, after the moon has been illuminated by the sun even with a single point. [Unclear] and it can come about that the diligent knower may succeed without the guidance of a teacher. Yet I think this is to be understood only in this book, and in none of the preceding ones. Concerning the following ones, judgment will be given in its proper place. Among all the cabalistic methods of secrets that we have given up to the present, the easier progression of this fourth book can be extended to infinity. Therefore it is enough that I have handed down to those desiring fuller things both the form and the reason of an example. This light of understanding easily penetrates all things. I wrote at Peapolis, on the ninth day of March, in the year of the Lord 1508.

[illegible]<Initial type="decorated-drop">C</Initial>EMONSTRATIONE possibilitatis nostrae quam breuiter nec minus sufficienter ostensa, non arbitror me ipsum in eadem hac uice diutius fatigandũ cũ iter modus praestet in infinitum, si cui ad ulteriora fuerit exemplar necessarium. Minime quoqꝫ reor necessariũ ea quae suu̇t recitata in praecedentibus ad memo riam reducere, cũ lector sagax si fuerit studiosus etiam que in his maiora latitant possit auxiliante domino inuenire. Materiam sapienti et amp; studioso tradidimus simul et amp; causam quibus si prudenter uti uoluerit, suo nostrum ingenio supe rabit. Quisquis uero hanc statam cupit in umbra pulchri orem, ingenio manũ coniungat et amp; animũ, &amp; iter sibi faciat ipse paraphrasmate pulchrius decoratum. Memoria tene at fixum si quẽ ista delectant ut in orbe semper maneat pre stituto, quẽ quolibet modo praetergressus fuerit, operatio tota inutilis euanescit. Hominũ plura sunt nomina, sunt de niqꝫ infinita pene uocabula rerum, uillarum, ciuitatũ, pro uinciarum, berbarum, lapidum et amp; uerborũ, quae nostris omnia subseruiunt institutis. Ex his libro mo dũ fieri constat nõ impossibile, si cũ diligentia sit praesto in genium, quae nostra inuenta praecellant in infinitum. Qui uero tante fuerit hebetudinis ut haec puerilia nostra intelli gere nequeat, ea quae subtiliora restabunt quando penetra bit: Finẽ libro polygraphiae quarto imponimus, cui quin tum in nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi sociamus</Line>Finis adest libri polygraphiae quarti, Ioannis Tri temij abbatis, xiiij. die Martij, anno M.D.VIII.</Line>

Once the demonstration of our possibility has been shown as briefly, and no less sufficiently, as possible, I do not think that I should weary myself longer in this same matter, since the method provides a path without end, if anyone should need an example for further things. Nor do I think it at all necessary to recall to memory the things that have been set out in the preceding pages, since a keen reader, if he is studious, will also be able, with the Lord’s help, to find the greater things that lie hidden in them. We have handed over to the wise and studious man both the material and the cause; if he wishes to use these prudently, by his own talent he will surpass ours. But whoever desires this arrangement to be more beautiful in its shadow, let him join hand and mind to talent, and make for himself a path more beautifully adorned by paraphrase. Let anyone whom these things delight keep firmly in memory that he must always remain within the prescribed circle; if he passes beyond it in any way, the whole operation vanishes uselessly. There are many names of men; finally, there are almost infinite words for things, villages, cities, provinces, herbs, stones, and words, all of which serve our purposes. From these it is clear that it is not impossible for a book to be made according to the method, if talent is present with diligence, which may surpass our discoveries without limit. But he who is of such dullness that he cannot understand these childish things of ours, when will he penetrate the subtler things that remain? We set an end to the fourth book of the Polygraphy, to which we join a fifth in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Here is the end of the fourth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot, on the fourteenth day of March, in the year 1508.

Καὶ ἄφεσθαι τὸν οἶμον τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ἐγγύτητιν, καὶ τὰς ἐπιτροπὲς τῶν ἱερέων καὶ τὰς παρατήρησιν, Τὰς δὲ ἰερὰς ἡμερομηνίας καὶ ὁδοὺς καὶ βουλευτικοὺς καὶ πολιτικοὺς, καὶ τὰς αὐτοψίας καὶ γῆν καὶ ψυχρᾶν καὶ νερὰν Παρὰ τὴν εἰσβολὴν· μὴν σὺν τῷ λόγῳ. Of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James the Apostle [unclear], Book Five of the Polygraphia: beginning of the chapter.

Those things which, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have set forth, as best we could, in the four preceding books for the completion of our Polygraphia, reasonably require that in the fifth book we briefly treat the remaining precepts and methods of this instruction that are left over. We shall therefore give in it a sufficiently concise method by metathesis, that is, by the transposition of letters, by which a friend may write securely, safely, and most secretly to a friend whatever he wishes. We read that Caesar Augustus used this manner of writing in secret matters. This method of sending messages, although in many ways secure, is nevertheless always regarded as suspect by those who look upon it, because as soon as a transposition of letters is seen, anyone curious immediately suspects that something lies hidden beneath them. But the methods of this invention are almost infinite; from them we have marked out the following for the reader as a necessary introduction, reserving the rest to be searched out by his own ingenuity. First, therefore, we have put before him the standard table of this practice, to which we have added a second, reversed one. In these two tables the root and foundation of the aforementioned transposition are wholly laid down, upon which the structure of the whole edifice is placed. For once these two tables have been properly known and understood, no transposition of letters will be able to escape one who works diligently. To these we have joined the order of twenty-four alphabets. The use of these, as one wishes, consists in each individually, or, if you prefer, even in all of them. If you have secret dealings with many people, assign individual alphabets to each of your confidants, while you commit to memory what you have given to each one. Let the first alphabet be entrusted to the first person, the second to the second, the third to the third, and so on with the rest. But if, because of a very great number of affairs or of associates, the alphabets which we have marked out should not suffice for all things, or if some of them seem too open and obvious, we shall be able to introduce various new transpositions, whose number may be very great, while the method of the secret always remains perpetually hidden. Let us give an example of this matter: let B be a, f be b, l be c, p be d, t be e, z be f, c be g, m be h; and so let it be done consequently through the whole customary alphabet, so that between any chosen letter three lie idle and transposed. Afterwards four, then five, more or fewer, yet in such a way that the whole alphabet, as though revolved in a circle, comes together, and no letter at all is omitted, but each one is placed in its own order in the same sequence for another. In whatever way you write, that very method must be firmly entrusted either to writing or to memory, lest, having slipped through forgetfulness, you can no longer read what you yourself had written. For the transposition of letters can be varied in so many ways that, according to the estimate of human understanding, which, enclosed by temporal operation in a mortal body, does not properly grasp infinities, there will arise for a mortal an innumerable number. Hence whoever wishes to have more methods of writing by metathesis, apart from our instruction, if he is even a little ingenious and diligent, will easily achieve the effect in his work. For the mind of man can do very great things if it is aided by study; but art that despises the smallest things never reaches the greater. I know that there will be very many who will mock these studies of ours as vain and childish; to them we give this answer: that we shall be entirely content provided they please those at whose request they were composed by us. The straight table follows.

quid unicuiqꝫ tradideris Primo quidē alphabetū cōmittatur primū: secundo secundum: tertio tertiū, & ita consequēter fiat de reliquis. Quod si praemultitudine negociorū autfamiliae alphabeta quae signauimus nō sufficerēt ad oīa uelsi aliqͣ ex eis nimis uidcant̉ patula manifesta, uarias trāspositiones nouas poterimus inducere, quarū numerussit maximus, arcani modus ꝑpetuo maneat semꝑ occul¬tus. Cuius rei ponamus exemplū: B fit a,f sit b,l sit c,p sitd,t site,z sit f,c sit g,m sit h, ita consequenter per totū alphabetū usuale fiat ut inter quālibet literā assumptā tresinteriaceant ociose atqꝫ transposite. Postea quatuor, deindequinqꝫ, plures aut pauciores, ita tn̄ q̃ totū alphabetū quasireuolutū in orbē concurrat, litera nulla penitus obmittatur, sed unaquaeqꝫ eadē serie pro alia in ordine suo collocetur.Qualicūqꝫ modo scripseris ipsum aut litteris aut memoriae tenaciter noueris cōmendandū, ne pͥ obliuionē lapsus,quod scripseras ipse legere iā nō possis. Tot em̄ modis litesrarum transpositio uariari potest, quod secundū estimationē intellectus humaniqꝫ operatione temporali conclususin corpore mortali nō capit proprie infinita, mortalis confurget numerus innumerabilis., Vnde quicūqꝫ modos scribebendi per metathesin plures habere uoluerit nostrainstitutione remotos, si uel parum fuerit ingeniosus diligens,facilē in operatione sua cōsequetur effectū.Maximaenim potest ingeniū hominis si studio iuuetur arteaūt spernit minima,nunqͣ pertinget ad maiora.Scio pleroqꝫ futuros qui haec studia nostra ut uana puerilia deridebunt, quibus damus pro responso,nos omnino fore cōtentos modo illis cōplaceant,ad quorum sunt instantiam a nobiscomposita. Direct table of transposition.

[table of letters and numerals]

multiplied the same number of times, they make a little less than fourteen thousand.

Reverse table of transposition.

[table of letters and numerals]

In this reverse table, you have just as many alphabets through the transposition of letters as in the preceding one, which we also set down as the direct table. For, as you see, under metathesis there are twenty-four toward the right. Likewise the same number toward the left; downward, twenty-four; and upward, ninety-eight. Multiplied four times twenty times, reduced in the form of a cross to the four sides, they make no fewer than one hundred and twelve alphabets.

The same table follows, expanded.

First figure of the expansion of the direct table.

[expanded table of letters]

This is the first figure of the expansion of the direct table: five alphabets by metatheses, as is seen, with transposition of the letters. For in the first alphabet b is taken for a, c is taken for b, and so on consecutively, as is clearer to one who looks closely. In the second alphabet g is taken for a; in the third, d; in the fourth, e; in the fifth, f, as the placement of the order teaches.

The expansion is continued.

Second figure of the expansion of the direct table.

[expanded table of letter-pairs]

In this second figure of the expansion of the direct table there are likewise contained five alphabets in number, from which by metathesis many others also can be made; their arrangement, for the sake of brevity, we have omitted. [unclear].

The expansion is continued.

This is the first figure of the expansion of the reversed table, which, since it proceeds from the opposite direction against the regular one, is deservedly called irregular. For, with the alphabets alternated in order, it introduces an error backward from the twelfth, and not in [unclear], nor [unclear]. Since the rule had given this, he did not think it should be altered. Continuation.

In the present orchema a manifold alphabet is handed down, by transposition and leap, both according to the rule of order and according to the position of the letters. All these things are sufficient as an example for those who cannot be content with fixed ones, so that they may have a method and form for discovering the rest, since they can be varied without number.

ii

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot [unclear], to the reader, greeting.

Since all the letters of the Greeks and Hebrews are numerical, I have often wondered that the inquisitive Latinity of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews, by doubling certain letters, established twenty-eight signs sufficient for every number. The Greeks, however, with like foresight relieved this lack of letters by the addition of four characters. Since we therefore have twenty-four letters, why do we not also make our own numerical, seeing that we can similarly find four doubled letters? Let us give four as an example, and all will be sufficient for number: final m and n; likewise closed v and open u. When we add to these the twenty-four usual letters, we have characters sufficient for all twenty-eight numbers. And it will be no matter of very great labor to commit this number to memory.

For this invention of ours will be able to be useful to many, since in number it comprehends many thousands in few letters, all of which at first glance, without any calculation, can be discerned and understood more clearly than light. Many who are less experienced in the art of calculation think that this cannot be done so easily by the figures of algorism, especially in large numbers. For as soon as you have looked with your eye upon any number, however great, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. Since this is done so easily, it is fitting that we mark the letters themselves reduced into number. Written 16 [unclear] 1508.

IOANNES TRITEMIVS ABBAS PEAPO LITANVS LECTORI S. <Initial type="decorated-drop">C</Initial>VM LITERAE Graecorum et amp; Hebraeorũ oẽs sint numerales, sepe miratussum quod curiosa priscorũ latinitas etiam suas literas numerorũ rationi subseruire non fecit. He braei quarundã duplicitate literarũ, notas octo et amp; uiginti ad omnẽ numerũ sufficien- tes intituerunt. Graeci uero huncliterarũ defectũ quatuor ap positione characterũ simili prouidentia subleuarunt. Nos er- go cũ w literas quatior habentes et amp; uiginti, quare et amp; nostras nõ facimus numerales, q̃ similiter quatuor possumus inueni- re duplicatas: Demus quatuor in exemplũ, &amp; satis omne erit ad numerũ, m et amp; n finale. item v clausum et amp; u apertum. His dum xxiiij. i iteras usuales adiungimus, octo et amp; uiginti numeris suf ficientes omnibus characteres habemus. Eritqꝫ baud magni laboris negociũ hunc numeri memoriae cõmendauerint. Poterit enim haecnostra inuentio multis esse proficua, quoni- am paucis literis multa milia cõprehendit in numero, quae o- mnia primo intuitu sine calculatione aliqua luce clarius discer- ni possunt et amp; intelligi. Quod fieri per figuras algarismi praeser- tim in numeris magnis tam facile non posse multis uidetur mi- nus in arte calculatoria expertis. Mox enim ut oculo numerũ quantũlibet magnũ inspexeri eum et amp; plene intelligere, &amp; ex- primere poteris sine circumlocutione seu diuisione sermonis. Quod quã fit facile cõueniẽs ẽ ut iteras ipsas in numerũ reda- ctas cõsignemus. Behold, reader, you have the method by which you can adequately mark down and write every writable number with a few letters; their range, as you see, proceeds to infinity. But, as people once used to say in a proverb, “The weary ox plants his foot firmly”: whoever wishes there to be a limit to the preceding things, let him follow the ancient method.

We have thus far set forth, by way of example, the ancient manner of the Franks of Germany in writing numbers with Latin letters, so that we might also provide knowledge of it to those who do not know it. But the fact that, in setting down the figures of algorism, we have departed from the common rule of computation was done not by mistake but for a reasonable cause, namely so that we should not be burdened by an excessive progression. There were also some who wrote larger numbers in this manner.

With these matters concerning the method of numbers duly completed, we also bring the fifth book of the Polygraphia to an end. In the year of the Lord 1508.

The sixth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James the Greater the Apostle at Würzburg, begins.

Before every invention and use of letters, in the beginning of the world, when human beings were still rough in understanding and uncultivated in manners, under the governance of a succession shared among three, as certain persons think, of intelligences succeeding one another in order for one thousand sixty-three years, the influences of the planets were in the world, acting in their own way upon bodies on earth. The ancient investigators of this matter say that Saturn, from the beginning of the world, presided by his influence over the things sprouting and growing on earth, principally through the governance of his intelligence, which they called Orifiel, that is, the life-giving one of God, for three hundred fifty-four lunar years, likewise four months, and as many days and hours. These things we recount as poetic; we do not affirm them.

After Saturn, Venus, and after Venus, Jupiter is held to have assumed dominion. After Jupiter, however, Mercury, fourth in order as ruler, adorned the talents of human beings with various arts. But under the three intelligences mentioned, namely while Saturn, Venus, and Jupiter were ruling, they assert that human beings did not have the use or knowledge of letters. Hence whenever one person wished to announce some secret to another, he did so not by writings, since the function of letters was lacking, but symbolically, by certain likenesses of animals, trees, plants, or other sensible things, according as each had agreed among themselves.

The age of Saturn, as they say, gave human beings manners suited to the influence proper to it. For it made farmers, hunters, founders of cities, rough men, woodland-dwellers, gloomy men, simple men, uncultivated in life and manners, living in the flesh for a long time. After Orifiel of Saturn, as those who hold such opinions say, the intelligence Anael, mover of Venus, received the governance of the world by influence for three hundred fifty-four

Ludos, cantilenas inuenerunt, citbara canere coepe runt, & quicquid ad veneris confirmant pertinere influentiā, mo- tum carnis nimiū sequentes studiosius excogitabant. Tertiā Io- uis intelligentiam nominabant zacharielem, quae dominiū susci- piens mundi post anaelem fecit homines dominandi cupiditate inquietos, uenationes agere, tentoria facere, & seuarijs indumen- tis exornare. Facta est eo dominante pro Iouis qualitate, qui pa- trē regno priuauit, magni inter bonos et malos diuisio, illis deū iuocantibus, istis uero carnī deditis et mundo. Fuerūt au- tem aliae literae tunc, ut referūt, ab his quas mundus hodie habet multū diuerse, ad formā et similitudinē arborum, plantarum et animalium excogitate, quae tamen cum tꝑe postea multipliciter sunt immutate, faciliorēqꝫ formandi modū sumpserunt et ornatū cultiorē. Mercurium em̄ figmenta poetarū omnis litterarae prae- sidem esse dixerunt, magna latere sub fabulis rerum arcana pro- mittentes. Humano postbęc multiplicato genere, & in omne ter- rā ubiqꝫ diffuso, non diu mansit unitas literarum, sed corporū et animorū procul ab inuicē diuisio, diuersos et uarios inuenit mo- dos scribēdi, de quibus longa nobis narratio. Plato philosoph⁹ in Phedro, literas usumqꝫ scribendi, simul et rationē ponderum, numerorum et ludum alearum quendā philosophū Theutonem

[unclear], months, days, and four hours; under him human beings began to be more cultivated, to build houses more frequently, and cities, and also to invent various manual arts, namely weaving, wool-working, and many other things similar to these. They also began to sink more deeply into the pleasures of the flesh, to take beautiful wives, and, when many children had been begotten from them, they notably fell away from natural simplicity. They invented games and songs, began to play the lyre, and whatever they declare to pertain to the influence of Venus they devised rather eagerly, following too much the impulse of the flesh.

They named the third intelligence, that of Jupiter, Zachariel; taking up dominion over the world after Anael, it made men restless with desire for ruling, to engage in hunts, to make tents, and to adorn them with various coverings. While he held sway there came about, in accordance with the quality of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, a great division between the good and the evil: the former calling upon God, the latter given over to the flesh and the world. Under that rule Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once.

The fourth mover, or angel of Mercury, Raphael, after Zachariel, pouring influence upon worldly affairs, began in the year of the world 1055 at the end of February, and lasted until the year 1410; under him the use of letters is said first to have been invented. At that time, however, the letters were, as they report, different from those which the world has today, devised in the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet afterward, with time, they were changed in many ways, and took on an easier manner of forming and a more cultivated ornament. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the presiding deity of all literature, promising that great secrets of things lay hidden beneath fables.

After this, when the human race had multiplied and had spread everywhere over all the earth, the unity of letters did not long remain; rather, the division of bodies and minds far from one another found diverse and various modes of writing, concerning which there is a long narrative for us. Plato the philosopher, in the Phaedrus, relates that a certain philosopher named Theuth first invented letters and the use of writing, together with the reckoning of weights, numbers, and the game of dice, and taught Thamus, king of the Egyptians. But concerning the other ancient men who are said to have handed down special letters to almost each nation and people, letters which remain in use among them down to the present day, it is not my purpose on this occasion to set down or indicate the narrative.

For all our teachers know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said first to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: α, β, γ, δ, ε, η, ι, λ, μ, ν, ο, π, ρ, σ, τ, ϖ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is reported to have added four: ξ, θ, φ, χ. And Pythagoras afterward added the letter v, so that there should be twenty-one. ζ, κ, and ω were subsequently invented by others. Jordanes, bishop of the Goths, gave letters proper to that people. When the unity of language had been confounded, the simplicity of characters too was varied in many ways.

Hence it came about that the use of letters, in the course of time, usurped such license for itself that not only individual peoples, but also individual men, fashioning new characters for letters at their own discretion, prepared hiding places for their mysteries. Yet every writing in an unusual character will not be free from suspicion among those who see it. Notwithstanding this, many kings, tyrants, and princes of old once devised for themselves a familiar mode of writing, separate from the common one, caring little for the suspicion of others, provided only that what they wanted to remain secret was not perceived. Moved by imitation of them, and desiring to bring this work of Polygraphy, as far as can be done, to a perfect conclusion, in this sixth book, which is also the last, I have resolved to call back from the dead certain characters of the ancients, which have long since passed out of mortal use, lest they perish altogether. And first indeed we shall set down the ancient mode of writing of the Northmen.

are referred, namely c, d, i, l, m, v, and x. The Normans, however, together with the Asiatic Dacians, having once come forth from the Scandinavian islands, which are now called Gothic, roamed through Gaul for more than forty years and devastated it most grievously. In order to provide for their secret affairs, as Bede the English monk bears witness, they devised from the letters of the Greeks a new and elegant method of writing of this kind. For they adapted the numbers of the Greeks up to twenty-four, comprised in ten letters, to Latin characters, and prudently hid our letters under a foreign form, namely in the way in which we use numbers in place of letters: that is, when for a we put 1, for b 2, for c 3, for d 4, and so on successively to the end of the alphabet. It was indeed a fine and sufficiently safe invention, which neither a Greek nor a Latin will easily understand. For the whole alphabet is not found in it, but only nine letters and one numerical sign, namely q̄, which among them signifies six; and in this manner of writing it stands for f, the sixth letter of the Latins. Furthermore, paying regard to our German tongue in which we were born, we have placed w, double, at the end as the twenty-fourth letter of our nation, which we have formed according to the Greek number thus: kδ. We shall set out this script of the Northmen from the following order of Greek letters, in imitation of them.

They represent the Latin letters, and they will be readable neither by a Greek nor by a Latin who has not first acquired knowledge of this device. This method of writing can also be varied in many ways, when the letters are changed by transposition of the number. This can be done in Greek letters in full, according to the chosen will of each industrious writer. Nor will the manner of forming these characters be very difficult, especially for one who has become somewhat practiced. The characters written above also suit the German language sufficiently well, since with them we can denote everything that occurs to us, in whatever speech we may be skilled. Whenever iota is placed by itself, so that it may be known to denote the letter k, the tenth of the alphabet, thus ĩ, it is marked above.

On the Alphabet and Method of Writing of the Ancient Franks.

The opinion of very many holds that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and they steadfastly affirm that they used the Greek language especially in their sacred rites. For they say that a great correspondence exists between the Greek language and our own, although the long interval of time has utterly extinguished that agreement. That most learned man, once my teacher, Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, had collected several thousand Greek words which signify the same thing in both languages, Greek and German. And Caesar testifies in the Commentaries that the ancient Druids, priests of the sacred rites in Gaul, used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. But when the Romans were laying waste the world, they at length violently imposed the use of their letters, together with their dominion, upon many nations. Finally the remnants of the Trojans, who were afterward called Franks, in the year before the incarnation of the Lord four hundred

Cumqꝫ testante Turpino, tam ardũ inchoasset opus, crebris bellorum incursionibus retartatus non perfecit, sed morte praeuẽtus imperfectum dereliquit, nec surrexit post eum alius qui huius rei curam ad animum revocaret. Otfridus autem iam dictus monachus Rabani Ful<Gap reason="damaged" extent="ca. 2 letters"/>ij

in the [unclear] fortieth [year], having gone out from the borders of the Scythians, with King Marcomer providing leadership, they came into Germany, and from their Saxon brothers received settlements at the mouths of the Rhine. Thereafter, waging war almost continuously with the Romans and Gauls for nine hundred and fifty years, as Hunibald is the authority, they finally brought almost all Europe under their empire or kingdom. Yet they did not abolish the letters of the Romans once they had received them, but rather, mingled among the Germans and Gauls, they learned their language, and preserved their letters and form of writing. Wasthald, a writer of the histories of this people, wrote in his native tongue books of the deeds of kings, dukes, and princes over almost seven hundred and fifty-eight years, with the following characters appended, as Hunibald says; he mentions them in his volume, which he published in eighteen books on the origin of the Franks.

Λα θε ϖν ζη υζ υβ φθ ξχ λι ρβ λγ ηι ιο χρ ψch Δδ θκ επ θτ πγ ϑς Λι βρ ∗πγ Εζ Ψμ στ ωω

Unless the fault of the scribe has deceived me, I have represented Wasthald’s alphabet suitably, as I think. In it some characters differ entirely from the Greek, while some also seem partly to resemble them. Yet I do not know what to judge: whoever their inventor was, although he did not keep the form of the Greek letters, he nevertheless observed the order of the letters. The manuscript, crumbling from excessive age, could scarcely be read; hence I fear that I have rather been deceived by some interpolator than found Hunibald’s true and certain meaning.

But let us pass on to what remains, since if Hunibald’s statement is true, it will have been well written by us; but if it is someone’s fiction, it will neither harm us nor do injury to the reader. There follows another fictitious alphabet found in Hunibald’s manuscript, to which this was inscribed:

The Alphabet of the Franks, which Doracus invented.

A Π F M ρ ζ q T φ Π b D h P n C r Δ w Π g Q i H n Ṗ s F ꝑ̄ Τ d E k A p η t X x Π c M l W ph b th X z

Whoever wishes to use the characters written above should know that they must be written below the lines in the manner of the Greeks, not above as the Latins do. Likewise it must be observed that, of double letters, the first are written at the beginning and in the middle of words, but the second always at the end.

From the grammars of Otfrid, monk of Wissembourg.

We read that Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Great, taking pity on the barbarous condition of his nation, with Nanno, Theobald, Albinus, and Berenger as helpers, attempted to give rule to the German language. And although, as Turpin bears witness, he had begun so arduous a work, he did not complete it, being hindered by frequent incursions of wars; but, forestalled by death, he left it unfinished, nor did another arise after him who would recall care for this matter to mind. Otfrid, however, the already mentioned monk, formerly hearer and disciple of Rabanus of Fulda, under Louis the Pious, son of that Charles, having mastered that grammar, however imperfectly, wrote many things in our German language, which seem to sound forth the admirable gravity of a regular instruction. For he worked out many poems according to that same rule, in heroic and also elegiac meter; moreover he composed some things also in prose to Louis, king of Germany, son of Louis the Pious and brother of Emperor Lothar; also to Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, to the monks of Saint Gall, and to others. Having obtained fragments of this grammar, I too have extracted the present characters from many, lest they should perish entirely. It is established, with Otfrid as witness, that Charles devised several alphabets of his own, which his very extensive kingdom might use securely in secrets with individual prefects. From these, with Otfrid supplying the letters, we commit these few things.

Charles the Great, king and most Christian emperor, fought for no less than thirty years with the Saxons, whom at last, overcoming them by the sword, he converted to the Christian faith. But fearing lest they should again apostatize from the faith, as they had done many times, he appointed certain secret inspectors, to whom he granted judicial power, who, traveling through all Saxony, were to inquire secretly and diligently concerning the faith and morals of the people; and whomever they found to have apostatized from the faith, robbers, adulterers, blasphemers, contemners of the church or of its priests and commands, or those [unclear] by notorious crimes the Christian

densis quondā auditor atqꝫ discipulus sub Ludouico Pio ipsi us Caroli filio grammatica illa quauis imperfecte cōsecutus multa scripsit in lingua nostra germanica quae regularis insti- tutionis mirandam sonare uidentem grauitatem. Carmina em̄ ad eādem normā lucubrauit plura heroico metro simul &; ele- giaco, insuper &; prosaice nõnulla composuit ad Ludouicum regem germaniae filium Pij Ludouici, &; fratrem Lotharij im- peratoris. Ad Otgarium quoqꝫ archiepiscopum Moguntinū ad monachos sancti Galli &; alios. Huius fragmēta gramma- tices assecutus &; ego praesentes characteres de mul- tis extraxi, ne penitus interirēt. Constat autem teste Otfrido Carolū propria plura excogitasse alphabeta, quibus perlatis- simum regnum secure uteretur in archanis cum singulis praefe- ctis. Veritus autem ne denuo sicut pluries fecerāt apostatarēt a fide, secretos quos- dā instituit exploratores, quibus iudiciariā contulit poꝛesta- tē, qui totā saxoniā peragrātes de fide ac moribus gentis secre- te īquirerēt diligēter, &; quoscūqꝫ reperissent apostatassea fide raptores, adulteros, blasphemos, ecclesiae aut sacerdotū eiꝰ et mādatorū cōtemptores, seu notorijs criminibus christiana rē R P [illegible]

disturbing the public [peace], or recalling or soliciting the people to paganism, they should without delay, by imperial and royal authority, hang them with a noose with impunity, or otherwise kill them as they could. And so that this institution might remain perpetually unshaken, he gave the same men the power of substituting also others, fit men under certain conditions, who, enjoying the aforesaid faculty, might with impunity exercise the office of inquiry and of death against the guilty. Finally he prescribed for them secret laws and hidden signs, together with a form of oath, by which they might proceed justly in judging and punishing, and, known mutually to themselves, might remain hidden from others, and might preserve perpetually in Saxon land the necessary judgment in greater secrecy. They also used certain alphabets among themselves for a time; these, however, at length fell entirely out of use. Yet the office of this sort of inquisition remains down to the present time, whose ministers are commonly called [felmeri?].

Although these characters do not appear sufficiently beautiful and elegant, nevertheless it has pleased me to join them with my aforesaid new inventions, for the honor and reverence of antiquity, since there is no one, even of slight industry, who cannot devise prettier ones for himself at his own discretion. Yet continued practice in writing will be able, by an easy correction, to amend this misshapen crookedness, and by frequent use to make it pleasing by habit. For no one, however learned or educated he may be, is a good writer in any language unless by long habit he has transformed the practice of writing into an art. Another also follows.

If anyone at his own discretion wishes to fashion a new alphabet for himself, let him know that two things especially must be observed, which nevertheless I do not always find preserved in the preceding examples. The first is that he form characters of easy drawing; and the simpler they are, the better they will be. The second is that he arrange the individual letters so that, when joined together into words, they present a beautiful and elegant appearance. I add a third, not promised: if you wish the writing to remain secret, make some letters of the alphabet double, after the manner of the Hebrews.

This Hichus the Frank came with Marcomer from the borders of Scythia to the mouths of the Rhine in Germany, and, as a supplement to the German language, is said to have invented these characters, which seem to agree sufficiently with it in many respects. Pharamund also, king of the Franks in Germany, the forty-third after Marcomer, who had brought in the nation, died in the four hundred twenty-sixth year of the Lord’s Nativity; when he had sent his scouts through Gaul for the purpose of invading it, he ordered them to write in such characters as these.

I have found also another alphabet, newly devised by a certain alchemist, which he was accustomed to use for hiding his secrets, forming a great estimate of his art, which contains little in itself besides words. For alchemy is loved by very many; she is chaste.

Alchemy has many domestic attendants, who guard their mistress with perpetual vigilance and put themselves forward under her name, so that they may preserve her forever untouched from intercourse with so many importunate lovers. Vanity, fraud, deceitfulness, deception, sophisticating, greed, lying confidence, foolishness, want, poverty, despair, flight, outlawry, and beggary are the handmaids of alchemy; while pretending that their mistress is loved, they guard her inviolate, and gladly prostitute themselves to the moneyed, avaricious, greedy, and silly seekers of her.

On the signs and wonderful, but excessively laborious, method of writing of Marcus Tullius Cicero, and afterwards of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, wrote a book of signs of no small size. Saint Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr, enlarged it with many signs and words, adding terms necessary for Christian uses, so that the work itself became useful not only to pagans, but much more also to the faithful.

The manuscript is rare; I have found it only once, and bought it at a cheap price. For when, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1496, I was examining many libraries out of love for books, I found the aforesaid manuscript in a certain monastery of our order, neglected because of its extreme age, cast away under dust and contempt. I asked the abbot, a doctor of law, at what price he valued it. He answered: he would prefer to it the little works of Saint Anselm, recently printed. I went to the booksellers, since the matter happened in a metropolitan city, and bought the requested little works of Anselm for one sixth of a florin; I gave them to the abbot, with the monks rejoicing, and freed the manuscript, which had already nearly been brought to destruction. For they had resolved, out of love for the parchment, that it should immediately be scraped.

Almost two years after this, I rode to Strasbourg on business of my order, and, being admitted by Johannes Keisersberg, the distinguished preacher of the place, into the library of the cathedral church, I found a psalter written wholly in the same signs of Tullius and Cyprian, and most handsomely written with golden capitals. But an inscription had been placed on the outside by someone ignorant of the mystery, as follows: “Psalter in the Armenian language.” I brought in a scholar, showed the falsity, and advised that it should be rewritten thus: “Psalter written in Ciceronian signs.” Whether he did so or not I am uncertain, because I did not afterwards return to that library. So that you may see, reader, the form of Cicero's notation, we have decided to append a few signs.

[unclear]

This method of writing requires great memory and an altogether immense labor of reading, since any character signifies either an entire word, or a final syllable, or some part of speech suitable for the composition of the whole. Therefore, omitting all the signs, let us draw an alphabet from a few:

W = a; X = c; F = k; [unclear] = o; [unclear] = s; [unclear] = y U = b; A = f; N = l; P = m; ph = z X = bb; G = [unclear]; [unclear] = m; PP = t; [unclear] = ph V = c; W = g; N = L; q = v; [unclear] = th Λ = cc; W = h; U = n; ψ = r; w = fp ν = d; Ψ = I; Λ = n; X = rr; x = st

Many other new alphabets could also be formed from the signs of Cicero; we leave their extraction to the judgment of anyone who wishes to undertake it. For the book is abundant, and contains many signs notably differing from one another, all of which serve writers.

This was the alphabet of Iaimiel, great king of the Artici, surnamed Megalopis, a very wise man, which he used in secret matters; it too can be altered in many ways. To it we also, out of love for our prince, have appended this one, in which writing, when more frequently used over time, will become easier.

we judge [it] to be of little usefulness. We fear that someday we shall be ashamed to have applied our mind to these trifles, while more useful matters were left aside. But, I pray, the readers will forgive me; for my own inclination indeed drew me back from these childish studies, not to say [unclear], vain ones, but the insistence of certain friends compelled me to write them, to whom I neither could nor ought to deny this without injury to the bond contracted. Nevertheless, led by their entreaty, I also had to join the following little chapter to the preceding ones, and to place numbers in place of letters. The ancients established various and multiple modes of writing by means of figures of numbers, by which, for subtle discovery, they safely transmitted their secrets to one another. Therefore, persuaded by the prayers of friends, we have placed at the end of this sixth book a few methods out of many, by which a way to knowledge of others may lie open to those who do not know them. For if anyone takes pleasure in knowing these things, he will easily be able, once these are known, to climb to higher things, and to vary the discovered methods in manifold alternation according to his own judgment. As a beginning for this matter we have placed a table beneath the figure, which, varied [unclear], will contain in itself an alphabet in the form of a cross, ninety-six.

causa nos mouente ratio/nis, quia cum sua progressione longius euagetur, labor men/tem perterruit immensus. Vnitatem quoqꝫnon locantes con/silio pertransiuimus, quam praeponere nostris adinuentis per ordinem temerarium iudicamus. Nam ex illis que iam exem pli causa ostendimus, qui est intellectui doneus maiora facile consequetur. Omnia ser uiunt arcanis.

The sixth and last book of our Polygraphy we have, by God’s mercy, brought to its close. In it, concluding our discourse with the wandering stars, we warn the reader in certain points. First, that as often as he uses an alphabet, he should prudently add the character or mark of some sign or planet, for the sake of a twofold usefulness. For by this means excessive labor is removed from the friendly reader, and the mystery will remain secret, since anyone ignorant of the craft, seeing a table written with numbers and marked beforehand with the characters of signs or planets, will think that it pertains to the method of astronomy, and will suspect that no mystery at all lies hidden. For this reason we have not begun [unclear] with the official letters, but from a distance, lest we give anyone occasion for suspicion. Nevertheless prudence must be used by writers, since an astute reader who is touched by suspicion of something hidden, if he detects the function of one number, will easily compute the whole alphabet.

Second, let anyone who desires to be a shrewd practitioner of this matter remember that whenever in any word a letter is doubled, as often happens, it should be written only once and marked above with a point. For example, I wish to write “Ioannes” from the alphabet of Aries: I do not duplicate 18, which is n, but write thus, 14. 19. 6. 18. 10. 23., “ioanes,” “abas,” so that every sign of suspicion may be removed. In similar cases similar caution must be exercised; for unless the practitioner is endowed with skill, and knows that greater things are to be found from small ones, he will not be a fit person to whom these very small matters of ours ought to be revealed. Not everything is to be communicated indiscriminately to everyone, especially things whose use can be turned to good and to evil. Moved reasonably by this consideration, we have plainly handed down in these six books of the Polygraphy many things to those who wish to know them, but we have allowed far more secrets to lie hidden beneath things manifest. Finally, we have written a key that lays open the whole work, showing how each metaphor is to be understood; yet by the counsel of certain men we have ordered it to remain hidden, so that studious persons may not lack material for exercising their memory, and that the cause of knowing it may be taken away from the wicked, who are not willing to use it well. In each passage many mysteries lie hidden, and the greater the things you discover from these, the more ample are those that remain to be found.

A way is prepared for beginners; for those who advance in it, it will not be difficult, in the course of time, to discover many rare and very great things. Here he who did not know how will learn to write Latin, and prudently to wrap all the mysteries of his will in a foreign language. But so that the ignorant man may be able to understand not only his own mysteries which he wraps up, but also open speech of which he has until now always been ignorant, the matter is not one of great labor, if the paraphrast has fully followed our intention in this volume. For beneath the bark lie the kernels of our Steganography, buried by just reason, lest they lie open to unworthy babblers. Finally it was worth the trouble that one work should not prejudice the other, but that its own right should be distributed to each unimpaired.

We, weary after a long voyage, here cast anchor in the sea under the name of JESUS CHRIST, the savior of the faithful, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1508, in the eleventh indiction of the Romans, at [Paeapolis?], a city of the eastern Franks, which they call Würzburg, Herbipolis.

The end of the sixth book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot at St. James in Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, is here.

Printed at the cost and expense of the most upright bookseller Johannes Haselberg of Aia, of the diocese of Constance, in the year 1518, in the month of July.

IMPRESSVM AERE AC IMPENSIS INTE GERRIMI BIBLIOPOLAE IOANNIS HASELBERGI DE AIA CONSTAN- TIENSI DI OECESIS, ANNO M. D. XVIII. MENSE IVLIO.

Preface to the explanation of the whole work of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James of Würzburg.

I trust that no one who reads these things will judge me either arrogant or superfluous because I myself have written a commentary on the Polygraphy recently composed by me, especially if he has been able to weigh precisely what reason induced us to speak obscurely. For whatever can do harm when made public had reasonably to be concealed in mystical language. But the subject that we treat in the Polygraphy is, for the advantage of the commonwealth among good men, very good, useful, and honorable; and for that reason, persuaded by a reasonable cause, we wrote it, so that by its service we might make good men safe and secure from the investigation of the wicked when they communicate their secrets to one another. But lest an opportunity be offered to the wicked and perverse, who even more frequently misuse good inventions, to deceive the simpler and those less cautious in judging matters, we handed down in it mystical or hidden methods of writing, and covered the truth lying hidden in the marrow with certain coverings of figures. Yet we do not at all doubt that any industrious man, eager with desire for these things, will easily grasp everything, if he applies even a modest persistence in searching them out. For the things I have handed down are neither so difficult nor enveloped in such great mysteries that they cannot be wholly penetrated by a studious man. For everywhere we have so tempered the riddles of our words that they may easily be accessible to learned and studious men, and nevertheless remain inaccessible to sluggish children of darkness. But after it pleased me to offer the very work of the Polygraphy, dedicated, to the most serene and most unconquered Caesar of the Romans, Maximilian, ever august emperor of the world, I thought it would be worthwhile if, with a few brief explanations, I should make it clear

112
Given these observations, I will provide a textual representation based on typical structure for such a document: [Blank Page] CLAVIS POLY GRAPHIAE IOANNIS TRITEMII ABBA tis diui Iacobi Herbipolensis, quondam Spanheimensis, ordinis sancti Bene- dicti, obseruantiae Bursfelden- sium patrum. Cum priuilegio de non imprimendo seu uendendo per alium in decẽ annis sub poena prout in literis. •IO. TRITHEMIVS• 83

open, lest the mind of his sacred majesty, which is daily stretched by many affairs and cares, be drawn back from understanding it by the obscurity of the mysteries. For unless my opinion deceives me, the work will be the more pleasing and useful to his majesty the shorter and clearer it is. First, therefore, with the Lord’s granting, we shall briefly explain the meaning of our proposal, which in the prologue is contained wrapped in various enigmas; then, through the individual books of the Polygraphy, we shall succinctly unfold, according to the powers of our talent, the methods of working, the rules, cautions, and differences, in the order in which they stand as necessary. All these things, so that they may more quickly become accessible to those who desire to know, we shall show one by one through examples, and we shall be as brief as the reasoning of the matter permits.

Key to the Explanation of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, [Paeapolitan?] Abbot.

Exposition on the Prologue.

Our whole intention in the entire work of the Polygraphy turns upon this proposition: that we should hand down certain methods of writing secretly, by which kings, princes, nobles and commoners, priests and laymen, the learned together with the unlearned, may secretly, safely, and without any suspicion of a hidden secret, communicate to one another, and to any friends, even those far distant from one another, by the service of letters, whatever conception of their minds they need, as often as there is need. And lest we seem to have presumed to be either the first or the only ones to do this, we give notice beforehand that many of the ancients long ago, especially tyrants, princes, and kings, moved by a similar consideration, devised for themselves familiar and various methods and canons of writing, by which they themselves attempted in particular what we have promised universally in our Polygraphy. From their number we first introduced, for the sake of the proposed example, Caesar Augustus; take his secret method of writing as thus [unclear].

Mystery. He changed the breathings of conceived speech, with [unclear] excluded, into obscure things; their barbarousness, resisting his wishes, he makes obedient to his nod by a certain fine invention, the scheme of transposition.

Explanation. That is: the great Caesar Augustus, in order to write secretly and safely what he wished, changed the letters of the alphabet by varied transposition, so that he put b for a, c for b, and so consequently for each. And so that the writing might remain more twisted and more secret, at his own discretion he transposed the letters breadthwise and lengthwise, at any distance of order, number, and place.

Mystery. And this receptive order, as though perpetual, subject to the will and to the reckoning of time, although it preserves messengers safe on the road from the attack of the [Bacuceans?], nevertheless, since it has no regulated bounds, makes all who encounter it anxious with suspicion of a hidden thing.

Explanation. Although no one can easily grasp with the understanding the secret mystery lying hidden under the transposition of letters, nevertheless this writing makes those into whose hands it comes suspicious about the hiding place of the thing enclosed.

Mystery. Archimedes, that Syracusan, easily the foremost of mathematicians, a white bird suited to his devices, bare through head and feet, etc.

Explanation. Archimedes had two little rods of one length and thickness planed round or square; one of them he kept for himself, the other he entrusted to his absent friend. And as often as one wished to write something more secret to the other, he wound the white bird, that is, a strip of papyrus of small width but of twice the rod’s length, around the wood and fastened it with wax below and above. Afterwards he wrote on the strip, along the sides, continuously upon what had been artfully joined together into a mass, whatever he wished; then he loosened the strip from the rod, and at once so great a distance appeared between the letters that not even one word cohered with another. He turned the strip when he wished; on the other side he wrote likewise. Nor was there anyone ignorant of this device who could have discovered the secret. But the man who had the other rod, when he had received the strip, attached it and restored the letters to their former order.

Mystery. Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, using art with talent, changed the minute parts of phrase into signs, etc.

Explanation. He wrote a book of signs for his son, which the blessed martyr Cyprian afterwards enlarged for the use of Christians, namely in the form of a dictionary.
